## Proof

Recall that a subset $V \subseteq \mathbb{R}^3$ is **Zariski closed** if it is the common zero locus of some collection of polynomials in $\mathbb{R}[x,y,z]$; that is, $V = \{p \in \mathbb{R}^3 : f_i(p) = 0 \text{ for all } i \in I\}$ for some family $\{f_i\}_{i \in I} \subseteq \mathbb{R}[x,y,z]$.

Consider the polynomial
$$f(x,y,z) = x^2 - y^2 z^2 \in \mathbb{R}[x,y,z].$$

This is a polynomial in three variables with real coefficients (it is the difference of two monomials, hence a well-defined element of the polynomial ring $\mathbb{R}[x,y,z]$).

The given set is precisely the zero locus of this single polynomial:
$$\{(x,y,z) \in \mathbb{R}^3 : x^2 - y^2 z^2 = 0\} = V(f).$$

By the definition of the Zariski topology on $\mathbb{R}^3$, the closed sets are exactly the algebraic sets — common zero loci of (arbitrary) collections of polynomials. Taking the collection to be the singleton $\{f\}$, we see that $V(f)$ is the zero locus of a family of polynomials, and is therefore Zariski closed.

Equivalently, $V(f)$ is the preimage of the closed set $\{0\} \subseteq \mathbb{R}$ under the polynomial (hence Zariski-continuous) map $f : \mathbb{R}^3 \to \mathbb{R}$, confirming that $V(f)$ is closed in the Zariski topology.

**Conclusion:** Yes, the set $\{(x,y,z) \in \mathbb{R}^3 : x^2 - y^2 z^2 = 0\}$ is Zariski closed, being the zero set of the polynomial $x^2 - y^2 z^2 \in \mathbb{R}[x,y,z]$.

### PROOF COMPLETE
